high_priority_articles.title: Malaysia Backs Myanmar’s ASEAN Return As Leaders Discuss Trade And Repatriation Of Thousands - Wake Up Singapore
high_priority_articles.summary: Malaysia Backs Myanmar’s ASEAN Return As Leaders Discuss Trade And Repatriation Of Thousands  Wake Up Singapore
high_priority_articles.full_text:
SUMMARY
- Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim voiced support for Myanmar’s return to full ASEAN participation during talks with Min Aung Hlaing.
- Both leaders pledged closer economic ties, with bilateral trade reportedly rising more than 140% year-on-year.
- Malaysia and Myanmar discussed repatriating thousands of Myanmar nationals held in Malaysian immigration detention centres.
MALAYSIA: Malaysia has pledged to strengthen ties with Myanmar and support its return to full participation in ASEAN, as the two countries discussed trade, investment and the repatriation of detained nationals.
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim met Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing in Putrajaya on Thursday during the Myanmar leader’s official visit.
At a joint press conference, Anwar said Malaysia recognised efforts by Myanmar’s government to improve bilateral relations and make domestic policy changes.
He also stressed that cooperation should focus on practical benefits for people in both countries, despite outstanding regional issues.
The discussions come as Myanmar’s military leadership has been excluded from high-level ASEAN meetings since the 2021 military coup, which triggered widespread conflict across the country.
Trade And Investment Take Centre Stage
Anwar said Malaysia wanted to expand cooperation with Myanmar across several sectors, including trade, investment, education, agriculture, energy, healthcare and skills development.
He noted that bilateral trade had increased by more than 140% year-on-year, although the statement did not specify the period or total trade value.
Myanmar is also seeking more foreign investment and fewer barriers to trade, according to Min Aung Hlaing.
The Myanmar president said his country wanted to develop into a major centre for trade and investment, highlighting economic, educational and cultural cooperation as priorities.
The two leaders’ discussions indicate an effort to strengthen economic links even as Myanmar’s political situation continues to affect its regional relations.
Thousands Of Detainees Could Return To Myanmar
Repatriation was another major issue during the meeting.
Anwar thanked Myanmar for accepting the return of more than 10,000 of its nationals at its own expense. He said such large-scale repatriation was uncommon among countries dealing with similar arrangements.
Myanmar also agreed to accept more nationals held in Malaysian immigration detention centres, provided their citizenship could be verified and the necessary arrangements completed.
Min Aung Hlaing said Myanmar wanted to bring verified citizens home as soon as possible. However, he stressed that officials must first assess the situation and make the required arrangements.
Malaysia completed the first phase of its voluntary repatriation programme on September 29, involving 1,476 Myanmar detainees.
A further 3,542 detainees have been agreed upon for the second phase, according to the Malaysian government, but a date has not yet been announced.
Displacement Remains A Major Concern
Myanmar’s crisis has forced thousands of people to flee since the 2021 coup and the ensuing conflict.
According to UNHCR figures cited in the report, Malaysia was hosting around 193,800 displaced people from Myanmar as of February, including Rohingya and Chin communities. Rights groups believe the actual number may be higher because many remain unregistered.
Min Aung Hlaing arrived in Malaysia on October 7 for a two-day official visit. His meetings with Malaysian leaders covered economic cooperation, regional engagement and arrangements for returning verified Myanmar nationals.
While the discussions point to closer bilateral ties, Myanmar’s wider conflict and its relationship with ASEAN remain important issues for the region.

high_priority_articles.summary: Treasury Yields Surge to Multi-Decade Highs as Fed Signals More Rate Hikes; Dollar Gains, Gold Slips  Tekedia
high_priority_articles.full_text:
U.S. Treasury yields climbed further on Thursday, with the benchmark 10-year yield approaching levels last seen more than two decades ago as investors absorbed a Federal Reserve warning that interest rates may need to rise again to contain persistent inflation.
The move higher in borrowing costs came ahead of a closely watched $22 billion auction of 30-year Treasury bonds, with investors looking for evidence that demand for long-dated U.S. debt remains strong even as yields rise and concerns over government deficits intensify.
The 10-year Treasury yield rose 4 basis points to 5.322%, after touching its highest level since 2002 on Wednesday before retreating later in the session. The 30-year yield increased more than 4 basis points to 5.705%, after trading just below a 24-year high in the previous session. The 2-year Treasury yield, which is particularly sensitive to expectations for monetary policy, rose nearly 3 basis points to 4.793%.

A basis point is one-hundredth of a percentage point. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions, meaning the latest moves indicate continued selling pressure across the Treasury market.
The immediate catalyst was the Federal Reserve’s latest meeting minutes, which showed policymakers expected another interest-rate increase before the end of the year to prevent inflation from becoming entrenched. Markets nevertheless expect the Fed to leave rates unchanged at its October 28 meeting, with investors assigning a substantially higher probability to another increase at the December 9 meeting.
Fed Governor Christopher Waller reinforced the hawkish message on Thursday, arguing that additional rate increases are needed to bring inflation back toward the central bank’s 2% target after roughly five and a half years of inflation remaining above that objective.
Waller, however, indicated that the Fed does not necessarily need to raise rates at every meeting.
“The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings,” Waller told a Central Bank of Turkey forum in Istanbul. “But they should be in place in an acceptable period of time.”
The Fed is signaling that policy may need to become tighter, but it is not necessarily committing to an uninterrupted sequence of rate increases. For Treasury investors, however, the prospect of rates remaining elevated for longer is enough to keep pressure on longer-dated bonds, particularly as the market reassesses how much compensation investors require to hold U.S. government debt.
Long-Term Treasury Demand Faces A Crucial Test
The Treasury’s $22 billion 30-year bond sale on Thursday represents the final major test of demand this week after auctions of shorter-dated securities.
On Wednesday, the Treasury sold $39 billion of 10-year notes, with global central banks accounting for more than 80% of the auction. That compared with an average of 72.4% for such auctions, providing an important source of support for the market despite the unusually high yield.
The Treasury also sold $58 billion of three-year notes on Tuesday.
“The 10-year auction has set the tone for the Treasury market – at least for the moment,” BMO Capital Markets’ Ian Lyngen said in a note late Wednesday.
Lyngen noted that the scale of the Treasury selloff between the September reopening and Wednesday’s auction might ordinarily have discouraged investors from bidding aggressively. Instead, the auction attracted strong sponsorship, even though it offered the highest yield on a 10-year Treasury auction since November 2000.
The focus now turns to whether that demand extends further along the yield curve.
Lyngen described Thursday’s long-bond auction as “the next barometer of demand for US debt in an environment of global deficit angst.”
That makes the auction more significant than a routine financing operation. Analysts say the U.S. government must now continue issuing large quantities of debt, while investors are demanding higher yields to absorb that supply. If demand remains firm even at elevated yields, the Treasury market could stabilize. If demand weakens materially, yields could rise further as the government has to offer greater returns to attract buyers.
The pressure is of the essence at the long end of the curve because 30-year yields incorporate not only expectations for near-term Fed policy but also longer-term inflation, economic growth, government borrowing and the compensation investors require for holding long-duration debt. The market will also receive the latest weekly initial jobless claims on Thursday and preliminary October consumer sentiment data from the University of Michigan on Friday, providing additional clues about the strength of the economy and the potential persistence of inflation.
Dollar Strengthens As Global Bond Selloff Widens
The Treasury selloff is also feeding directly into currency markets. The dollar moved toward its strongest level in 18 months on Thursday after the Fed minutes reinforced the view that inflation remains the central bank’s principal concern. Rising oil prices have added another complication by increasing the risk of renewed price pressures, while higher euro zone bond yields have weighed on the euro.
The dollar index rose 0.1% to 102.32 after gaining 0.3% on Wednesday. It remained only a few pips from its strongest level since April 9, 2025, when markets were still reacting to President Donald Trump’s so-called Liberation Day tariff announcement.
The euro fell slightly to $1.1191, close to its lowest level in 17 months.
The weakness of the European currency is not simply a reflection of dollar strength. Investors are increasingly concerned about fiscal and political conditions in France, where government bonds have come under pressure ahead of next year’s presidential election.
The spread between German and French 10-year government bond yields widened by 4 basis points on Thursday, reflecting a rising risk premium for French debt.
“If you look at euro-dollar, it’s not only about dollar strength but euro weakness coming from the political situation in France,” said Tommy von Brömsen, FX strategist at Handelsbanken.
That perspective matters because the global bond selloff is increasingly becoming a currency-market story. Higher U.S. yields make dollar-denominated assets more attractive, while fiscal concerns in Europe undermine demand for the euro. The result is a reinforcing cycle in which bond-market weakness contributes to currency weakness, particularly for economies facing greater fiscal uncertainty.
The dollar rose 0.1% against the yen to 158.22, reversing a brief decline following data showing that Japan’s current-account surplus reached 4.062 trillion yen ($25.7 billion) in August, above economists’ median forecast of 3.19 trillion yen.
The Australian dollar fell 0.1% to $0.6953, while the New Zealand dollar slipped 0.1% to $0.5592. The dollar was broadly unchanged against the offshore Chinese yuan at 6.7030.
Gold Caught Between Inflation Fears and Higher Yields
Gold, meanwhile, managed a modest recovery after suffering its sharpest pressure in weeks. Spot gold rose 0.3% to $4,122.99 an ounce by 0916 GMT after falling to its lowest level since August 5 on Wednesday. U.S. gold futures for December delivery gained 0.18% to $4,147.90.
The recovery came despite an increasingly difficult macroeconomic backdrop for the metal. A stronger dollar and higher Treasury yields raise the opportunity cost of holding gold because the metal generates no income.
The Fed minutes showed policymakers were divided over the case for another rate increase. Some officials believed higher rates were necessary to prevent energy and other price shocks from feeding into inflation, while a more hawkish group viewed further tightening as necessary to guard against emerging demand-driven inflation.
Markets currently assign only a 21.6% probability to an October rate increase but price in an 85% probability of a December hike, according to CME’s FedWatch tool.
“Prices are wobbling above $4,100 as geopolitics stoke inflation fears and year-end Fed hike bets,” said Lukman Otunuga, senior research analyst at FXTM.
He warned that a stronger dollar and higher Treasury yields could place further pressure on gold. Technically, he identified $4,100 as an important threshold, saying a sustained break below that level could expose the metal to $4,000, while holding above it could allow a rebound toward $4,200.
The conflicting forces are increasingly impacting gold. Geopolitical tensions and higher energy prices support demand for the metal as an inflation and uncertainty hedge, but the same inflation pressures can produce a more restrictive Fed, higher bond yields and a stronger dollar, all of which undermine gold’s appeal.
The latest shipping data add another layer to that tension. The number of vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz fell to its lowest level in more than two months after attacks on tankers in the strategic waterway reached their highest level last week since the start of the Middle East war. Any sustained disruption to energy flows could intensify concerns about another inflationary shock.
Other precious metals were mixed. Spot silver fell 2.2% to $58.8476 an ounce, while platinum rose 1.6% to $1,656.88 and palladium gained 0.8% to $1,133.65.

The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on Wednesday (October 7, 2026) raised the policy repo rate under the liquidity adjustment facility (LAF) by 25 basis points to 5.50% and shifted its stance to ‘calibrated tightening’ from ‘neutral’, signalling that rate cuts are off the table in the near term.
The sudden re-escalation of the West Asia conflict in September and the consequent hardening and volatility in global crude prices soured global economic sentiment and unsettled financial markets, the Governor Sanjay Malhotra said. On the rationale for the MPC’s decision, the Governor said, “The MPC noted that the global context on account of geopolitical developments remains challenging. Nonetheless, the Indian economy has been strong, and the economic momentum remains broad-based. Moreover, the economy is expected to remain resilient.”
The real GDP growth for FY27 is projected at 7.1%, while CPI inflation is now projected at 5.2%.

high_priority_articles.title: 'Every day there is killing': Gazans face Israeli strikes despite ceasefire as peace deal stalls - BBC
high_priority_articles.summary: 'Every day there is killing': Gazans face Israeli strikes despite ceasefire as peace deal stalls  BBCGaza ceasefire ‘exists in name only’, more than 100 NGOs say  Al Jazeera‘Neither war nor peace’: Palestinians in Gaza on existing amid disease, despair and ruins  The GuardianIsrael’s ‘scorched-earth’ ceasefire in Gaza  Financial TimesLife in Gaza still 'absolutely horrendous' - UN official  RTE.ie
high_priority_articles.full_text:
In her tent in central Gaza early one morning last month, 31-year-old Fida al-Toutah, a mother of five, was combing her daughter's hair when the sound of gunfire erupted.
"My mother shouted at us to get down," her son Ezz recalled, weeping as he spoke.
He only realised Fida had been hit when he saw the bloodied hands of his younger brother, who had been clinging onto his mother as the bullets came in.
"Our mother was so kind and generous. What did she do wrong?" Ezz said.
Fida died on 21 September from a gunshot wound to the head.
She is among more than 1,400 people in Gaza who have been killed in Israeli attacks since the start of the ceasefire on 10 October last year, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The ceasefire saw thousands of Palestinians held by Israel released in return for all of the 48 remaining hostages held in Gaza, and an agreement to end the war - which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage.
On the ground in Gaza, it meant that Israel's large-scale bombardment stopped, which brought substantial relief and an increase in humanitarian aid and medical supplies entering the territory.
But even during the ceasefire, Israel has continued launching strikes in Gaza almost every day. In the past week alone more than 30 people have been killed, according to Gaza's health ministry.
Israel says it is targeting Hamas operatives, and accuses Hamas of continued violations of the ceasefire.
"It [the ceasefire] is all lies. Every day there's a shooting. Every day there is killing and death lurking around," said Ahed, Fida's husband.
In response to the BBC's questions about Fida's killing, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said they had no record of the incident.
The total death toll from Israeli attacks since the start of the war in Gaza three years ago now stands at more than 74,000, according to the Gaza health ministry.
Outside Fida's tent, her brother Ibrahim pointed to the holes he said were made by a volley of bullets fired by Israeli forces.
"This tent is just a piece of cloth. Imagine that a military vehicle came down here and fired a spray of bullets," he said. "There was also gunfire coming from the sky, from above, from quadcopters, and it was directed at unarmed civilians."
Fida is the fourth of Ibrahim's siblings to be killed since the start of the war. "We left our neighbourhood Zeitoun to survive, but death is following us," he said.
The family has moved seven times but safety has been out of reach. Most of Gaza's 2.1 million population has been displaced multiple times by the war, the UN says, with many forced to live in tented cities and unsafe structures.
On the same day that Fida was killed, 14-year-old Ismail al-Bardawil was also shot dead. He was killed in the al-Mawasi area of Rafah, in southern Gaza.
His family told the BBC that he was shot by Israeli forces while he and his brothers were fishing in the Mediterranean Sea, around 20m (66ft) from the shore. He is one of more than 300 children killed since the start of the ceasefire, according to Gaza's health ministry.
The IDF said it had no information about this incident either.
Over the past year, the IDF has released videos of its operations in Gaza targeted at Hamas and other groups. At least seven Israeli soldiers have been killed in Gaza since the start of the ceasefire.
Both Fida and Ismail lived close to the so-called Yellow Line that separates the areas occupied by the Israeli military in Gaza from areas controlled by Hamas in the west.
Areas around the line are considered the most dangerous because Israeli forces have frequently opened fire there. But there are few options to move because there is an extreme shortage of space.
The strip was densely populated even before the war began. Now, its population is squeezed into under 40% of its area, which is controlled by Hamas.
In those areas the group maintains a tight grip, clamping down on dissent and still recruiting fighters.
In May this year, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he had directed the IDF to increase the area of Gaza under Israel's control to 70%.
Architect Amal Alabadla, who lived in a comfortable flat prior to the war, now lives in a tent on the coastline.
"Every time the rains come, it gets flooded. I feel very scared when the wind is strong because our tent gets destroyed or damaged," she said.
Amal is forced to raise her two boys - Mohammed and Noah - on her own.
Her husband was not in Gaza when the war broke out, and in three years they have not been reunited. Amal's three brothers, who helped her care for the boys, were killed in separate attacks before the ceasefire began.
"During the winter, my son suffers from epilepsy seizures because of the cold. It's very hard sometimes to keep him dry and warm," she said.
"Before the war, I had a job, a house, an ordinary life, but then everything turned upside down. Now we have no hope, nothing. It's only about survival day by day, to keep my kids alive, clean, healthy and fed."
There are camps further inland in Gaza that have even been built below sea level, which are at greater risk of flooding.
The October 2025 peace deal was supposed to pave the way for the reconstruction in Gaza, but rebuilding has not yet begun - stuck in limbo because of an impasse over the second phase of the deal.
Israel strictly controls what materials and machinery are allowed into Gaza, acting, it says, for reasons of its own security.
Earlier this year, US President Donald Trump put forward a plan to disarm Hamas, but in August it was rejected by Netanyahu, who stated that no military pull-out would happen until Hamas was "genuinely" disarmed.
Hamas has said handing over its heavy weapons is contingent on Israel ending "all forms of aggression" and withdrawing its forces from Gaza.
Half a world away, Trump's Board of Peace has also proposed a recovery plan for Gaza worth $2.45bn (£1.85bn).
But, one year on from the ceasefire and three years on from the start of the war, many like Amal are deeply sceptical of things actually changing on the ground.
"We are struggling and not being allowed to rebuild," she said. "I don't think they are telling us the truth about allowing us to rebuild a safe future for our children."
Additional reporting by Imogen Anderson and Malak Hassouneh

high_priority_articles.title: Fed minutes: Another rate hike likely coming this year to combat persistent inflation - Hartford Courant
high_priority_articles.summary: Fed minutes: Another rate hike likely coming this year to combat persistent inflation  Hartford Courant
high_priority_articles.full_text:
By CHRISTOPHER RUGABER, AP Economics Writer
WASHINGTON (AP) — Most Federal Reserve officials expect that another interest rate increase will likely be needed this year to combat inflation, according to minutes released Wednesday from the central bank’s most recent meeting.
The officials unanimously agreed that inflation was still elevated and had not made much progress toward their 2% target in recent months, the minutes said. The Fed increased its key interest rate at the Sept. 15-16 meeting by a quarter-point to about 3.9%, its first increase in three years.
The increase defied President Donald Trump’s repeated calls for the Fed to cut rates and prompted the president to criticize the Fed’s rate-setting committee, though he still expressed support for Chairman Kevin Warsh, whom he appointed earlier this year. The rate increase comes as Americans are already struggling with high costs for groceries, gas and housing, and as affordability has taken on a leading role in the upcoming midterm elections, just seven weeks away.
Longer-term interest rates for mortgages and other borrowing have also jumped in the past few months for a range of reasons, including rising government debt, heavy borrowing by tech firms to finance data center construction, climbing oil and gas prices, and signs that growth and inflation remain elevated. The Fed’s rate hike has likely played only a limited role in the increase.
Still, key policymakers have said since the meeting that the Fed can take some time to monitor the economy and the impact of last month’s rate hike before making another move. Wall Street investors now forecast the Fed will keep its rate unchanged at its next meeting Oct. 28-29, according to futures pricing, and raise it when they meet in December.
Philip Jefferson, vice chair of the Fed’s board of governors, said last week that policymakers “will need to come to our own judgement, which may take more time.”
Inflation, according to the Fed’s preferred measure, came in lower than many economists expected in August but remained elevated. Overall prices rose 3.4% compared with a year earlier, while core prices — which exclude volatile food and energy categories — increased 3%. On a monthly basis, prices rose 0.3% from July to August, and core prices just 0.2%.
According to the minutes, even with the rise in longer-term rates, many officials said that financial conditions—which includes rising stock prices — “appeared to be supportive of economic growth,” a sign that more rate hikes may be needed to cool the economy.
Several policymakers said that they saw the Fed’s rate as too low to restrain the economy, or only acting as a mild restraint. That suggests they would support multiple rate hikes to rein in inflation.
Higher oil and gas prices stemming from the Iran war and the lingering effects of tariffs have lifted costs in recent months. But even excluding those trends, many Fed officials believe inflation is stuck between 2.5% and 3%, above its target. Spiking prices for semiconductors, computer equipment, and electrical components due to the rapid surge in data center construction have also played a big role in accelerating inflation.
The Fed lifted its key interest rate to about 3.9% at its Sept. 15-16 meeting, its first increase in three years. Higher rates are intended to slow borrowing and spending, cool the economy and bring down inflation.
Warsh emphasized after the announcement that the economy has shown signs of gathering speed since the central bank decided to keep rates unchanged in late July.
“The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” Warsh said at a news conference after last month’s meeting. “We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective clearly and at sufficient speed. Today the FOMC decided that this standard has not been satisfied,” he added, referring to the policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee, an arm of the Fed.
Trump criticized the committee for voting to raise rates, calling them “very political,” but he did not single out Warsh.
“They’re raising rates to make Trump do as bad as they can possibly do,” the president said.

high_priority_articles.summary: The Philippines is optimistic about the possibility of finalizing the Code of Conduct in the South China Sea.  Vietnam.vn
high_priority_articles.full_text:
|  | 
| President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. during a discussion at the 24th Forbes Global CEO Conference on October 8th . (Source: Inquirer) | 
 According to The Inquirer , speaking at the 24th Forbes Global CEO Conference in Singapore on October 8th, Marcos acknowledged that negotiations on the Code of Conduct (COC) remain challenging, with persistent disagreements even on the interpretation and definition of common terms. However, he affirmed the parties' determination to reach an agreement, viewing it as a crucial tool for managing tensions in the region where overlapping territorial claims exist.
 According to the Philippine leader, a complete resolution of the disputes may not be possible in the near future, but the parties need to build effective dispute management mechanisms to avoid mistakes or misunderstandings that could lead to unintended confrontations. He warned that a mistake by a sailor or soldier could spark a wider conflict.
 President Marcos also emphasized the importance of maintaining peace and freedom of navigation in the South China Sea, a vital shipping lane for international trade.
 At the forum, the Philippine leader also explained that his country uses the name West Philippine Sea to refer to the waters that Manila identifies as belonging to the Southeast Asian nation's exclusive economic zone and continental shelf in the South China Sea. He cited the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) to affirm the Philippines' legitimate rights and interests in these waters.
 President Marcos's remarks come as ASEAN and China aim to complete COC negotiations by 2026. The Philippines, as ASEAN Chair, is pushing this process forward before handing over the rotating chairmanship to Singapore in 2027.
 ASEAN and China adopted the Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea (DOC) in 2022, but it is not binding, while negotiations on the Code of Conduct (COC) have dragged on for years.
 Last July, Philippine Foreign Minister Ma. Theresa Lazaro stated that ASEAN and Chinese negotiators had been holding monthly meetings since January. Remaining issues to be resolved include legal status, geographical scope, and the definition of key terms in the agreement.

Iran has sharpened its criticism of a Saudi Arabia-Pakistan-Turkey defense pact after it became operational, warning against intervention in Yemen and questioning Pakistan’s role as a mediator between Tehran and Washington.
The trilateral pact entered its operational phase on October 5 following an escalation in Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi infrastructure. Turkey and Pakistan said they had begun taking measures to support Saudi Arabia.
Under arrangements discussed by the three countries, Pakistani and Turkish forces are expected to provide military, technical and intelligence support to Saudi Arabia, including defensive capabilities inside the kingdom. Officials have said the forces will not take part in offensive operations in Yemen.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei, asked on Sunday about reports that tens of thousands of Pakistani troops could be deployed to Saudi Arabia, said: “We have also heard this rumor, and we hope it is not true.”
“The countries of the region are well aware that any intervention in the Yemen issue could have undesirable consequences for the region,” he added, expressing hope that pacts such as the Mecca agreement would not be used “against the interests and welfare of the Muslim community.”
The Saudi Arabia-Turkey-Pakistan defense pact, signed in August in Mecca, stipulates that an attack on any one of the three countries will be treated as an attack on all three.
‘Begging for security’
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, without directly referring to the pact, called on neighboring countries to pursue “self-reliance” and a policy based on “genuine brotherhood.” He also said such agreements would not constrain Iran.
Several lawmakers dismissed the pact as largely symbolic. Ahmad Bakhshayesh, a member of parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, called it a “paper and political pact.”
Sharper criticism came from committee member Ebrahim Rezaei.
“The Saudis should know that a paper agreement with Turkey and Pakistan will not bring them security, just as years of one-sided milking of the Americans did not bring them security,” he wrote on X. “Correct your policies so that you do not have to beg others for security.”
That tone has hardened as the pact has moved into its operational phase.
Alaeddin Boroujerdi, a member of parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, said Thursday that Turkish and Pakistani involvement in the Saudi conflict with Ansarullah, as the Houthis are formally known, would neither weaken the group nor restrict its ability to operate in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
“The entry of Pakistan and Turkey will definitely work to their own detriment,” he told ISNA. “They should learn from history ... Saudi Arabia once had a coalition with a large number of countries, but after seven years of war in Yemen, it was defeated.”
‘Regional intervenor’
Iranian criticism has focused more heavily on Pakistan than Turkey, in large part because of Islamabad’s prominent role in mediating between Tehran and Washington.
Lawmaker Ahmad Naderi wrote on X that “Pakistan’s entry alongside Saudi Arabia into the war against the people of Yemen … shows that Pakistan should no longer be considered a mediator but a regional intervenor.”
The Tabnak news website went further, saying Iran viewed the deployment of Pakistani forces to Saudi Arabia as a threat to its security and “will not tolerate Pakistan’s military presence for military operations in the Yemen war.”
It also warned that Pakistan’s increasingly overt alignment with Saudi Arabia could heighten sectarian tensions at home and bring instability to the Iranian-Pakistani border.
Conservative commentator Hassan Hanizadeh similarly accused Saudi Arabia of seeking to create a religious divide, describing a recent meeting in Riyadh involving Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish officials as a sign of “the formation of a Shiite-Sunni polarization in the region.”
Boroujerdi pointed to potential domestic opposition in Pakistan, saying its people were “revolutionary, Muslim and highly sensitive to such issues” and that Islamabad would not have an easy path if it entered the war.
‘Alliance against the oppressed?’
Iranian state media have adopted a more confrontational tone as the pact has become operational, while giving extensive coverage to warnings from Houthi officials directed at Turkey and Pakistan.
Tasnim described the development as “Turkey and Pakistan join the Saudi war against the Yemeni people,” while Nour News, which is close to Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, asked: “Mecca alliance or alliance against the oppressed people of Yemen?!”
In a Thursday commentary, Tasnim warned that if Ankara and Islamabad participate in attacks on Yemen, “they may be directly harmed through attacks on their ships, interests and perhaps even their own territory.”

high_priority_articles.title: Vietnam’s industrial park profits fall 40% in H1 despite FDI surge: report - Theinvestor
high_priority_articles.summary: Vietnam’s industrial park profits fall 40% in H1 despite FDI surge: report  Theinvestor
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Vietnam’s industrial park developers are struggling to convert a surge in foreign investment into higher profits, as slower land handovers, rising costs, and changes in revenue recognition weigh on earnings, according to SSI Securities.
The country attracted $50.4 billion in registered foreign direct investment (FDI) in the first nine months of 2026, up 76.4% year-on-year. Meanwhile, net profit among industrial park developers fell 40% in the first half, the report released on Thursday said.
Manufacturing and processing remained the largest recipient of newly-registered FDI capital, accounting for 45.8% of the total. Singapore and South Korea led, with shares of 31.7% and 19.5%, respectively.
Disbursed FDI reached $21.1 billion in January-September, the highest level in the same period in five years.
However, the strong inflow of foreign capital has yet to translate into stronger earnings across the industrial property sector.
SSI Research’s industry data showed that net revenue among industrial park developers fell 20.2% year-on-year to around VND38 trillion ($1.47 billion) in H1/2026. Net profit dropped more sharply, declining 40% to VND4 trillion ($154.7 million).
Becamex IDC Corp. (HoSE: BCM) reported revenue of VND1.66 trillion ($64.2 million), down 65% from a year earlier, while net profit fell 82.7% to VND320 billion ($12.38 million).
Kinh Bac City (HoSE: KBC) recorded a 46% decline in revenue to VND1.93 trillion, with after-tax profit dropping 79.2% to VND260 billion. Sonadezi Chau Duc Corp. (SZC) reported revenue of VND234 billion, down 63%, and net profit of just VND36 billion, down 83.7%.
SSI Research attributed the weakness mainly to the absence of large-scale land sales recorded by some developers in the previous year, alongside higher interest expenses. Changes to revenue recognition, including the allocation of revenue over time, also weighed on reported earnings at companies such as SZC and Sonadezi Corp. (SNZ).
Performance diverges
Not all developers experienced a downturn. Idico Corp. (HoSE: IDC) posted net profit of VND1 trillion ($38.67 million), up 20.2% year-on-year, while Viglacera Corp. (HoSE: VGC) recorded VND1.15 trillion ($44.48 million), up 37.5%. Improved land leasing and a recovery in demand for construction materials supported their results.
The divergence highlights why rising FDI does not immediately translate into higher profits for industrial park developers. Earnings depend on the timing of land handovers, revenue recognition, and the characteristics of individual projects, analysts at SSI Research noted.
Meanwhile, leasing activity has shown signs of recovery. Net industrial land absorption in northern Vietnam reached 217 hectares in the second quarter of 2026, the highest level since Q1/2024. In the south, net absorption stood at 67 hectares, compared with just 10 hectares a year earlier.
Average industrial land rents continued to edge higher, reaching $143 per square meter per lease cycle in the north and $185 in the south, up 2.9% and 3.7%, respectively.
Rising development costs, however, are weighing on the profitability of new projects. Construction material prices have increased by an average of about 20%, while compensation and site clearance costs remain a challenge.
SSI Research estimates that profit margins for new industrial parks have fallen to 30-35%, well below the more than 50% achieved by existing parks.
Outlook improves for 2027
Looking ahead, SSI Research forecasts that new lease contracts and memorandums of understanding signed by companies under its coverage will total 1,000 hectares in 2027, up 18.6% year-on-year.
Combined net profit for industrial park developers and rubber companies involved in land conversion is projected to reach VND22.3 trillion ($862.44 million), up 12.4%.
SSI Research highlighted the potential of VGC and IDC, citing strong operating cash flow that supports their ability to maintain cash dividend payments.
Viglacera is forecast to deliver the strongest profit growth among companies covered by SSI, with earnings projected to rise 29% in 2027. Growth is expected to be supported by new industrial parks, including Song Cong II and Tran Yen, as well as existing projects such as Phu Ha, Thuan Thanh, and Yen Phong IIC.
For Idico, continued profit growth in H1 and its cash-generation capacity underpin SSI’s positive assessment.
SSI Research also maintains an optimistic view of rubber companies GVR, PHR, and DPR, as compensation income from the conversion of rubber plantation land is expected to remain a driver of earnings.

SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won visited the planned site of South Korea's Honam National Semiconductor Industrial Complex for the first time on the 9th, formally announcing a so-called "early groundbreaking" strategy under which SK Hynix would begin fab construction first, even if critical infrastructure such as power and water supply is delayed. The move is widely interpreted as a strong commitment to a speed-driven approach, accepting substantial upfront construction costs rather than waiting for infrastructure completion in order to respond to explosive AI demand.
Chey visited the planned ammunition depot relocation site at Gwangju Military Airport at approximately 2:50 p.m. that afternoon, stating, "We expect semiconductor demand to grow at a considerably rapid pace," and adding, "We need to accelerate the pace of expansion." He was accompanied by SK Hynix CEO Kwak Noh-jung and Jeonnam-Gwangju Integrated Special City Mayor Min Hyung-bae.
Chey made clear that accelerating the existing Yongin cluster timeline alone is not enough. "We've pulled forward Yongin's completion date by 12 years, but that alone is insufficient," he said. "Another site needs to be developed, and it must be pursued in parallel." Regarding the purpose of the site visit, he explained, "It's to assess how quickly we can build facilities here."
The specific groundbreaking date for the Honam fab has not yet been finalized. However, Chey laid out a blueprint to dramatically shorten the overall project timeline by running the national-level power and water supply plans concurrently with SK Hynix's construction. "Demand is growing at a rapid pace, so supply speed must also increase," he said. "Once we determine that conditions allow construction, we will make decisions quickly."
Notably, he unveiled a bold plan to preemptively begin construction if infrastructure development threatens to delay fab construction. "Once construction begins, we will push forward at the fastest possible speed," he emphasized. "If power and water are delayed and timing slips, we will proceed with groundbreaking first. We will not spare construction costs."
Chey also left open the possibility that the investment scale could expand beyond initial plans. "Currently, the Honam semiconductor cluster is planned at roughly two-thirds the scale of Yongin," he said. "If there is additional land demand, this site could grow larger." The remarks suggest that beyond the two fabs currently planned, additional capacity expansion could follow depending on market conditions.
The 800 Trillion Won Investment Plan and Remaining Challenges
On June 29, the South Korean government, SK Hynix, and Samsung Electronics announced plans to invest a total of 800 trillion won (approximately $597.3 billion) to build four semiconductor fabs in the Gwangju Military Airport area, with Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix each responsible for two fabs. This marks the first time Chey has personally visited the Honam industrial complex site.
On this day, Chey and his delegation received a briefing on site conditions from officials of the Air Force's 1st Fighter Wing, followed by a presentation from Jeonnam-Gwangju Integrated Special City officials on infrastructure development plans including power and water supply and permitting. They then spent approximately 15 minutes touring the ammunition depot relocation site to assess actual site conditions.
The Gwangju Military Airport site consists of 6.13 million square meters for Gwangju Airport, 770,000 square meters for the ammunition depot relocation site, and 1.3 million square meters of other land. The government and the Integrated Special City are pursuing a plan to first develop approximately 2.08 million square meters—including the ammunition depot relocation site and areas where landowner concerns have been resolved—out of the total 8.2 million square meters designated for the national industrial complex. The site was designated as a candidate for the Honam National Semiconductor Industrial Complex on July 29, and Korea Land & Housing Corporation (LH) is currently conducting design-related services for the complex.
The current schedule calls for completing tenant agreements, permitting, design, and partial site preparation by the end of next year, with groundbreaking to begin in 2028 once the military airport site is handed over. If the timeline holds, initial semiconductor production would be possible by June 2030.
However, significant administrative procedures remain, including the relocation of Gwangju Airport's domestic flights to Muan International Airport, the dispersal of military units, the lifting of military protection zone designations, and the formal designation and site preparation of the national industrial complex. The Integrated Special City plans to expedite administrative support, including permitting and infrastructure construction, to align with corporate investment timelines.
Accelerating Competition for Supply Chain Dominance
Chey's remarks are widely seen as a strategic decision by SK Group to pull forward production capacity expansion as global semiconductor supply chain restructuring accelerates. Beginning fab construction without waiting for infrastructure completion increases upfront investment burdens, but the calculus is that it secures supply in time to meet surging AI semiconductor demand.
With the judgment that pulling forward the Yongin cluster's completion by 12 years is insufficient to absorb growing demand, the plan is to rapidly elevate Honam into a second production hub. By leaving open the possibility of expanded investment, Chey signaled to the market that the Honam cluster could grow into a core production base rather than merely a supplementary site.
SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics have been in discussions with relevant agencies including the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport, the Ministry of National Defense, and the Jeonnam-Gwangju Integrated Special City over fab site selection. With Chey personally visiting the site and signaling a speed-driven approach, negotiations with the government and local authorities over permitting and infrastructure development are expected to accelerate.

high_priority_articles.full_text:
As more ASEAN member states engage Myanmar leader Min Aung Hlaing, analysts say the growing contact is raising questions about the bloc's unity and the future of the Five-Point Consensus.
SINGAPORE: Malaysia's efforts to re-engage Myanmar and support its eventual reintegration into the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) come amid a broader increase in engagement between the bloc’s member states and Myanmar leader Min Aung Hlaing, observers say.
Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim on Thursday (Oct 8) pledged that he would do “whatever is possible” to strengthen cooperation and bring Myanmar back into the ASEAN fold.
Malaysia is the fifth ASEAN member state to host Min Aung Hlaing since he took office in April, after visits to Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam and Laos.
Analysts say the growing engagement raises questions about the bloc's unity and the future of the Five-Point Consensus.
Moe Thuzar, senior fellow and coordinator of the Myanmar Studies Programme at Singapore's ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, acknowledged the need to keep communication channels open, but warned against allowing dialogue to come at the expense of compliance and accountability.
Hunter Marston, director of the Southeast Asia Program at Australian think-tank The Lowy Institute, also noted that Malaysia's outreach to Myanmar appears to be driven partly by domestic political considerations.
"The push stems from Anwar's coalition's recent electoral losses in Johor and Negeri Sembilan in July and August, which have prompted increased pressure on Anwar to act in response to popular opposition to the hosting of Rohingyas in Malaysia,” he said.
Rohingya Muslim refugees have been facing increasing harassment and scrutiny in Malaysia amid a surge of online hate speech and misinformation.
Malaysia has also said it can no longer take in refugees from Myanmar, saying they had become a financial burden and a security risk.
Anwar confirmed on Thursday that 10,493 Myanmar nationals had been repatriated so far this year and he has also vowed to push for Myanmar to accept Rohingya refugees.
While Malaysia’s position is that the visit does not amount to recognition of Myanmar's military-backed government, analysts say the growing number of ASEAN member states engaging with Min Aung Hlaing risks weakening the bloc's collective pressure on Myanmar and could further complicate efforts to uphold the peace plan.
"That increasingly divides ASEAN," Marston said, adding that countries such as the Philippines, Singapore and Indonesia may find themselves in a “very uncomfortable position”.
He added that this also leaves the Five-Point Consensus – which all ASEAN countries, including Myanmar, agreed to in 2021 – in a “very tenuous position”.
ASEAN's Five-Point Consensus
Following a 2021 military coup, ASEAN has excluded Myanmar from high-level meetings as it has yet to make meaningful progress on the bloc's Five-Point Consensus to end hostilities.
During a meeting in April 2021, all ASEAN leaders reached a consensus about the situation in Myanmar.
The five points are:
First, there shall be immediate cessation of violence in Myanmar and all parties shall exercise utmost restraint.
Second, constructive dialogue among all parties concerned shall commence to seek a peaceful solution in the interests of the people.
Third, a special envoy of the ASEAN chair shall facilitate mediation of the dialogue process, with the assistance of the secretary-general of ASEAN.
Fourth, ASEAN shall provide humanitarian assistance through the AHA Centre.
Fifth, the special envoy and delegation shall visit Myanmar to meet with all parties concerned.
Experts say that for Myanmar, the benefits of engagement outweigh the cost of taking back thousands of its nationals from Malaysia as it seeks to restore its standing within ASEAN and strengthen regional economic ties.
“It's a small price to pay really for the de facto recognition that comes with a state visit to Kuala Lumpur. Malaysia literally rolled out the red carpet for Min Aung Hlaing,” Marston said.
“This is the normalisation that he is seeking within ASEAN. This is part of the long-term play to restore Myanmar's recognition … restore trade and intra-regional connectivity to get the economy of Myanmar back on its feet.”
Marston noted that ASEAN's official position on Myanmar has not changed despite the growing number of member states engaging Min Aung Hlaing.
He pointed to comments by Philippine Foreign Minister Teresa Lazaro, who has said the Five-Point Consensus remains the bloc's preferred roadmap for Myanmar.
Marston added that Singapore appears poised to continue a similar approach when it assumes the ASEAN chairmanship in 2027.
MYANMAR LEADERSHIP SEEKING LEGITIMACY
Thuzar also said that diplomatic outreach is part of a concerted push by Myanmar’s military leadership to gain greater acceptance within the region after years of diplomatic isolation.
"The optics that we're seeing out of this recent visit (to Malaysia) indicate that Naypyidaw is going to milk any diplomatic mileage that it can get out of it," she told CNA.
Thuzar noted that Myanmar has traditionally prioritised bilateral diplomacy, using ties with individual countries to advance its regional interests.
She added that Min Aung Hlaing's overseas visits have often included business delegations and investment-focused engagements, underscoring efforts by Myanmar’s leadership to attract economic support amid ongoing instability at home.
ENGAGEMENT VS COMPLIANCE AND ACCOUNTABILITY
While acknowledging the need to keep communication channels open, Thuzar warned against allowing dialogue to come at the expense of compliance and accountability.
"There's no denying the need for dialogue and communication," she said.
"But I think the nuance that we probably need to look out for in the coming weeks and months is compliance and accountability.”
She added that these considerations are crucial if ASEAN wants to maintain its position on implementing the Five-Point Consensus.
She also pointed to the need for continued engagement with other Myanmar stakeholders, including the National Unity Government (NUG), Myanmar’s main opposition organisation which views itself as the country’s legitimate government.
Malaysia had previously stressed the importance of maintaining such balance, Thuzar noted.
The question for ASEAN, both analysts suggested, is whether growing bilateral engagement with Myanmar can be reconciled with the bloc's long-standing position that meaningful progress on the Five-Point Consensus is needed before the country can be fully reintegrated into the regional fold.

high_priority_articles.title: Gold prices drop 26% as Fed rate hikes offset geopolitical demand - PravdaReport
high_priority_articles.summary: Gold prices drop 26% as Fed rate hikes offset geopolitical demand  PravdaReport
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Gold prices in 2026 have undergone a significant correction, shifting the asset from a perceived bubble zone toward a range more suitable for long-term accumulation. Between January and October, the price of the metal dropped from a historic peak of $5,595 per troy ounce to $4,130, representing a 26% decline from the high and a 20% drop from February levels, which fluctuated between $5,180 and $5,230.
This downward trend has evolved from a technical pullback following the rapid gains of 2025 into a reaction to fundamental macroeconomic pressures. The primary driver is the shift in U. S. monetary policy; the Federal Reserve's September decision to raise interest rates to a range of 3.75-4.00%, combined with expectations of further tightening, has increased the yield on U. S. Treasuries. Because gold provides no yield, rising bond returns diminish its relative attractiveness to investors.
Adding to this pressure is a complex interaction between energy markets and inflation. Conflict in the Middle East has driven up oil prices, fueling inflationary expectations. This environment restricts the Federal Reserve's ability to lower rates, effectively trapping gold in a high-rate regime. This mechanism was particularly evident in September, when the asset lost approximately 6.6% of its value. This pressure is further compounded by a strengthening U. S. dollar, which weighs on the XAU/USD exchange rate.
Despite the price contraction, the structural drivers of long-term demand remain intact. Geopolitical instability, the pursuit of reserve diversification by emerging markets, and a general decline in trust toward dollar-denominated assets-accelerated by the freezing of Russian reserves-continue to support the metal. Demand from central banks and exchange-traded funds (ETFs) also remains a persistent baseline.
Given these conditions, attempting to time the absolute bottom remains risky, as a 20% decline does not inherently signal a floor. A more measured approach involves scaling into positions based on specific risk tolerances:
| Gold Portfolio Weight | Objective and Strategy | Risk Profile | 
|---|---|---|
| 5-10% | Baseline position: inflation hedge, protection against geopolitical shocks, and currency diversification. | Conservative | 
| 10-15% | Increased allocation: deliberate expansion of the defensive component during the correction. | Moderate | 
| 15-20%+ | Active bet on precious metals. | Aggressive (acceptance of potential further drawdowns of 15-25%) | 
For investors operating in rubles, the calculation is further complicated by currency volatility. The total return is dictated not only by the XAU/USD chart but also by the ruble-dollar exchange rate, meaning a 20% correction in dollar terms may not translate to an equivalent discount in local currency.
While the retreat from peak valuations creates a more attractive entry point for gradual accumulation, the Federal Reserve's high-interest-rate stance remains the primary constraint. This suggests that a rapid return to January's record highs is unlikely in the near term.

high_priority_articles.title: U.S. Probes EU Carbon Border Tax’s Effect on Trade and USMCA - Dakota News Network
high_priority_articles.summary: U.S. Probes EU Carbon Border Tax’s Effect on Trade and USMCA  Dakota News Network
high_priority_articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The Trump administration is asking U.S. companies and workers to document how the European Union’s new carbon border fee is affecting their sales, a step that could lay the groundwork for trade enforcement against one of America’s largest trading partners.
The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative published a request for comments in the Federal Register on Thursday, Oct. 8. It seeks input on the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, known as CBAM, and on European proposals that would extend the charge to hundreds of additional steel- and aluminum-based products.
Among the questions USTR wants answered: whether the program puts American producers at a disadvantage against European or other foreign competitors, and “whether and what enforcement action may be appropriate” to remedy any harm. Comments are due Nov. 9.
The notice lands as Washington is also renegotiating its trade relationship closer to home. In July, the U.S. declined to extend the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement during a mandatory review that USTR launched with its own Federal Register notice last year. Both reviews bear on the same industries, including steel, aluminum and the goods made from them.
How the carbon fee works
The EU enacted CBAM in 2023 to put a carbon price on certain imports equal to what European manufacturers pay under the bloc’s Emissions Trading System. It currently covers aluminum, cement, electricity, fertilizer, hydrogen, and iron and steel.
EU importers of those goods must report the greenhouse gas emissions generated in making them and buy CBAM certificates priced off the trading system’s auctions. The program moved from a reporting-only transition into full operation Jan. 1, 2026, according to the USTR notice.
Importers will not have to pay until September 2027. But goods entering the EU since Jan. 1 are already building up obligations based on their embedded emissions.
The European Commission sets the certificate price from the trading system’s auctions. It was 82.32 euros per metric ton of carbon dioxide for the third quarter, up from about 75 euros in the first half of the year, according to the Commission. Certificates for 2026 imports go on sale in February 2027.
Foreign producers can supply verified, company-level emissions data. Otherwise, importers must use EU default values, which USTR says carry a deliberate penalty markup meant to push companies toward submitting their own data. Any company data must be checked by an EU-accredited verifier.
Proposals to widen the net
In December 2025, the European Commission proposed adding more iron and steel products and a new category of combined metal products covering more than 100 downstream goods made largely of steel and aluminum. The plan also included anti-circumvention rules.
The EU’s other two lawmaking bodies went further. The Council of the EU adopted a position in June that would add more than 300 products. The European Parliament voted Sept. 15 for a version adding about 400.
The three institutions must now reconcile their versions in negotiations known as trilogues before final approval, which USTR said could come later this year.
Europe’s case, and its critics
Brussels says the fee is meant to keep factories and their emissions from simply relocating to countries with weaker climate rules, and to put European and foreign producers on the same carbon footing.
The Commission also says CBAM complies with World Trade Organization rules. In a Dec. 17 statement, it described the program as a “climate-oriented, environmental policy tool which will be applied in a non-discriminatory manner,” S&P Global reported. That report also said China’s Commerce Ministry warned on Jan. 1 that it would respond to what it called unfair trade restrictions.
Europe’s steel industry wants the program to go further. Lawmakers approved the Parliament’s expansion plan 464-50, with 159 abstentions. Ahead of the vote, Eurofer Director General Axel Eggert said the region’s mills are “investing billions to produce cleaner steel” and need a level playing field, Eurometal reported.
Russia has taken the fight to the WTO. It filed the first formal challenge to CBAM in May 2025 and asked for a dispute panel in July after the EU declined consultations, Interfax reported. Russia’s Economic Development Ministry called the program “a discriminatory tool that the EU uses to unlawfully restrict access to its market.”
What’s at stake for U.S. exporters
The United States has no national carbon price, so American shippers of covered goods get no credit for carbon costs already paid at home.
The administration has objected to CBAM before. In April 2025, USTR listed the program among foreign practices it considers unfair, and the administration estimated it would affect about $4.7 billion a year in U.S. exports, Argus Media reported. That figure measured trade exposed to the fee, not the fee itself.
Outside analysts put the direct bill much lower. The Niskanen Center, a Washington think tank, projects U.S. goods entering the EU will owe roughly $231 million in CBAM charges this year, rising above $250 million in 2027. Iron and steel account for $121.6 million of that and fertilizers $103.9 million.
Most of that cost comes from default values. Almost every U.S. exporter will be charged at the EU’s higher default rates in 2026, Niskanen said, partly because too few EU-accredited verifiers are available. With verified actual emissions, the same shipments would owe about $55 million to $65 million, it estimated.
“None of that money has to leave this country,” wrote Niskanen’s Jia-Shen Tsai. He argued the U.S. could collect the revenue itself through a domestic carbon price or an emissions accounting standard Europe would accept. Congress’s fiscal 2026 spending bill directed the Energy Department to study the carbon intensity of U.S. products covered by CBAM, the group noted.
The new notice asks for specifics: affected products, trade values, lost sales, job impacts, compliance costs and the size and location of affected producers. USTR said it is especially interested in effects on small- and medium-sized businesses and on indirect exports, such as U.S. parts that end up in goods shipped to Europe.
The agency said the comments will inform its continued engagement with the EU on the program.
The North American backdrop
The CBAM review runs alongside a separate, larger trade fight on the continent.
On Sept. 17, 2025, USTR published a Federal Register notice seeking public comment on the operation of the USMCA ahead of the pact’s first six-year joint review. It held a public hearing Nov. 17, 2025, at the U.S. International Trade Commission in Washington, as required by the law that implemented the agreement.
When the three countries met July 1, 2026, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the United States “did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form.” Greer said the agreement remains in force while Washington presses Mexico and Canada over its trade deficits with them.
Mexico and Canada both supported a 16-year extension, according to International Institute for Sustainable Development reporting. Because no extension was confirmed, the countries now hold annual reviews. The pact will expire July 1, 2036, unless all three agree to extend it.
The U.S. has pursued separate bilateral talks rather than three-way negotiations. Its talks with Mexico have covered steel, aluminum and derivative products, among other issues, the same family of goods the EU is moving to add to CBAM. As of late July, the U.S. had held no formal rounds with Canada, IISD reported.
What it means for agriculture
Fertilizer is the farm sector’s most direct exposure to CBAM. Nitrogen fertilizers such as ammonia have been among the covered products since the program began. Crops and food products are not covered.
That has blunted a recent win for U.S. ammonia producers. The EU dropped its 5.5% tariff on U.S. ammonia under a trade deal the European Parliament approved June 16. But U.S. ammonia faces CBAM charges of up to $196 a metric ton under the EU’s default emissions values, compared with about $59 to $62 for supplies from Egypt and Algeria, Fertilizer Daily reported, citing Argus Media.
The gap stems largely from U.S. plants that use petroleum coke rather than natural gas as a feedstock. Analysts do not expect U.S. ammonia shipments to Europe to grow significantly before 2027, when producers that can verify lower plant-level emissions could cut their charges.
The EU has already eased the rules somewhat. It cut the penalty markup on fertilizer default values from 10% to 1% through 2028, citing production costs and food security, Niskanen noted. Even so, U.S. shipments of ammonia, urea and other nitrogen fertilizers still face a nine-figure bill this year, by the group’s estimate.
The fee is also squeezing European farmers. January reports indicate that growers expected higher input costs as importers pass along CBAM charges. After lobbying by French and Italian agriculture ministers, the EU suspended its standard import duties on ammonia and urea for one year starting May 30.
Europe’s own fertilizer makers support the fee and oppose exempting their products. In April, their trade group, Fertilizers Europe, urged the EU to send CBAM revenue to farmers instead. “Farmers need direct financial support, but not at the expense of EU production,” said Aviv Bar Tal, chief commercial officer at OCI Global and a Fertilizers Europe board member, S&P Global reported. A Commission spokesperson said then that the EU had no plans to exempt fertilizers.
Broader U.S. farm exports to Europe have not been hit directly. They reached a record $14.5 billion in 2025, led by corn and tree nuts, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture.

high_priority_articles.full_text:
Switzerland is being gradually integrated into a broader European security architecture increasingly oriented towards possible long-term confrontation with Russia, writes Uroš Lipušcek.
By Uroš Lipušcek
Special to Consortium News
The Protection of Swiss Neutrality referendum, which Swiss voters overwhelmingly rejected on Sept. 27, appeared, at first sight, to be a vote on a very specific Swiss question: whether the country’s traditional neutrality should be defined more precisely and strictly in the Constitution.
The referendum was an immediate effort to stop Switzerland from joining European Union sanctions against Russia, and honor only U.N. Sanctions, and to prevent the country from entering into cooperation with a military alliance unless Switzerland is attacked.
The broader question is whether Swiss neutrality has become so flexible that it risks losing its strategic meaning? What does the referendum’s defeat mean for neutrality as an element of a future European security architecture?
Despite deep historical roots, Swiss neutrality was not formalized in the 1848 Federal Constitution.
The initiators of the Sept. 27 referendum called for a much more precise constitutional definition of neutrality, intended to prevent the government’s current and highly flexible interpretation of neutrality, which allows Switzerland to move increasingly closer to NATO’s security doctrine.
The referendum raised a fundamental question that is important not only for Switzerland but for all European states: what does neutrality actually mean in 21st-century Europe?
Can a state be simultaneously neutral and closely integrated into Western security structures? Can neutrality be used selectively, à la carte — as a legal principle, a security strategy, an instrument of foreign policy and at the same time an element of national identity?
The result was very clear. 70.15 per cent of voters rejected the initiative, while 29.85 per cent supported it. All 26 cantons rejected the proposal.
Voter turnout was 47.07 per cent, meaning that approximately 33 per cent of all eligible voters actually voted against the initiative. Switzerland has no minimum turnout requirement for a federal referendum to be valid. According to the Swiss federal authorities, average turnout in referendums is around 46 per cent.
Turnout in this referendum was therefore slightly above the long-term average, although the relatively low level of participation may also reflect the repeated assurances by the government and the leading media that the referendum was not a vote on abolishing neutrality, but merely on whether a stricter and more restrictive form of neutrality should be written into the Constitution.
Neutrality as a Binding Principle
Swiss neutrality has a tradition stretching back several centuries.
The Old Swiss Confederacy had been an expansionist power between 1470-1516 in which it fought the Habsburgs, the Burgundians in the 1470s, the Swabians in 1499 and the Italians, pushing into Lombardy, leading Machiavelli to compare the Swiss to the Romans leading Machiavelli to compare the Swiss to the Romans and a Macedonian Phalanx. The Italian campaign ended with the defeat at Marignano in 1515 and the 1516 Treaty of Perpetual Peace with France, which led to the origins of Swiss neutrality.
The first formal declaration that the confederacy was a “neutral estate” came in 1674 in a resolution of the Tagsatzung (a diet of envoys from the 13 cantons).
The Old Swiss Confederacy collapsed when Napoleon’s troops invaded and established the Helvetic Republic, a French-dominated centralised state. This episode demonstrated an essential fact: neutrality alone could not protect Switzerland if the European balance of power collapsed.
At the 1815 Congress of Vienna, the victorious European powers over Napoleon agreed that a permanently neutral Switzerland was in the interests of European stability and it was internationally recognized. This remains an important geopolitical fact even today. Switzerland became one of the principal examples of a permanently neutral state operating within this legal framework.
The First World War
The First World War pitting France against Germany provided a dramatic test of Swiss neutrality. Joining one side could have threatened Switzerland’s internal cohesion among Swiss, French and German speakers.
Neutrality therefore became not only a foreign-policy principle but also a mechanism for holding together a multilingual and multi-confessional society.
The Second World War
The Second World War was the greatest test of Swiss neutrality to that time. Surrounded by Axis-controlled powers, Switzerland maintained formal neutrality. It mobilised its armed forces and developed defensive plans designed to make an invasion costly.
At the same time, the history of Swiss neutrality during the Second World War remains highly controversial. Switzerland maintained extensive economic and financial relations with both sides and made significant concessions to Nazi Germany. Its banking system and trade policy have subsequently been subjected to extensive historical investigation and criticism.
The Cold War
After 1945, Swiss neutrality entered a new phase. Switzerland remained outside both NATO and the Warsaw Pact. During the Cold War, neutrality gave Switzerland a distinctive diplomatic position.
Geneva became an important centre of international diplomacy and humanitarian activity. The International Committee of the Red Cross, the European headquarters of the United Nations and numerous international organisations developed a major presence in Switzerland. Neutrality therefore became an important diplomatic asset.
The Post-Cold War Period
After the end of the Cold War, Switzerland began to reconsider neutrality in a more flexible and pragmatic way.
In 1991, Switzerland participated in economic sanctions against Iraq. In 1996, it joined NATO’s Partnership for Peace, although it did not join NATO itself. In 1999, it sent unarmed personnel to support international peace-building efforts in Kosovo. In 2002, Switzerland joined the United Nations. In March 2025, it joined NATO’s Science and Technology Organization – Enhanced Partnership.
In December 2025, the Swiss government announced that Switzerland and NATO had established a cooperation programme for 2025–2028, aimed, among other things, at increasing the interoperability of the Swiss armed forces, including its air force and communications systems.
Switzerland has therefore repeatedly adjusted its interpretation of neutrality to changing international circumstances since the end of the Cold War.
The Referendum Proposal for Stricter Neutrality Criteria
The initiative, supported by the Swiss People’s Party (SVP) and organised by the group Pro Switzerland, demanded a considerably stricter constitutional definition of neutrality.
In its view, neutrality should be defined as “permanent and armed.” Switzerland should not join any military or defence alliance, nor cooperate with such an alliance, except if Switzerland itself were attacked or an attack against it were directly imminent.
Had the initiative succeeded, Switzerland would have been constitutionally committed to a much stricter interpretation of neutrality, under which the continuation of sanctions against Russia, for example, not authorised by the U.N. Security Council, would have become legally and politically far more difficult.
According to the initiators, Switzerland’s increasing rapprochement with NATO and its policy of confrontation with Russia have therefore moved the country away from strict neutrality.
What Does Neutrality Mean under International Law?
International law determines how a neutral state must behave during a war between other states. The Hague Conventions of 1907 stipulate that neutral states must not allow foreign troops or weapons to cross their territory and must not provide military assistance to belligerent parties.
This does not mean, opponents of the initiative argued, that a neutral state must be politically or economically indifferent to every international conflict or violation of international law.
Even before the Second World War, Switzerland adopted what became known as “differential neutrality.” It remained exempt from military action but accepted certain economic sanctions imposed by the League of Nations.
Switzerland’s participation in League of Nations sanctions against Fascist Italy in 1935 became an important historical example of what was then called “differential neutrality.” The modern Swiss debate concerns whether such differentiated neutrality remains legitimate when sanctions are not collectively authorised by the U.N. Security Council.
The Confrontational Geopolitical Climate in Europe
Because of the growth of a perceived Russian “threat“ to Europe, Switzerland has increased its military expenditure with the rest of Europe. By 2032, the military budget is expected to rise from approximately CHF 6.3 billion, or 0.7 per cent of GDP, to 1 per cent of GDP.
For 2028–2030, the Swiss government intends to earmark additional revenue generated by a 0.5 percentage-point increase in VAT specifically for defence spending. This is expected to generate approximately CHF 1.7 billion in additional funds annually during those three years.
In August this year, the Swiss government also approved an additional CHF 970 million for military expenditure, particularly for air defence and protection against drones. In addition, the Swiss government has estimated that another CHF 24 billion will be required exclusively for weapons procurement projects.
The combination of a higher regular military budget, additional VAT revenue and the extraordinary procurement programme represents a substantial increase in Swiss defence expenditure.

Despite India and the U.S. narrowing their differences, trade talks have hit a roadblock. According to BMI, a Fitch Solutions company, a breakthrough in the near future is unlikely as negotiations remain ongoing.
Bilateral trade talks were initiated following a meeting between Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and U.S. President Donald Trump in 2025, with the goal of achieving $500 billion in bilateral trade by 2030. By February 2026, New Delhi and Washington had announced a basic framework for an interim trade agreement.
However, in October 2026, Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said that negotiations for a final deal had reached a “plateau,” with further concessions being “very, very difficult” for both nations, according to Reuters. Amid persistent roadblocks and delays, the prospect of an interim trade deal is offering hope for progress in bilateral ties.
“We expect India and the US eventually to conclude a narrow interim trade deal, although the remaining differences make a near-term breakthrough unlikely,” BMI said in a report on the status of the India-US interim trade agreement, according to Business Standard.
Vision Times reporter Venus Upadhayaya spoke with Dr. Ram Singh, Professor and Head of the Centre for Distance and Online Education (CDOE) at the Indian Institute of Foreign Trade in New Delhi, about the causes of the impasse in trade talks and what to expect next.
