Vision Times: India and the U.S. are unlikely to see a major advance in trade negotiations in the near future, as the two sides remain split over market access, agriculture, purchase of U.S. goods, and India’s procurement of Russian oil, according to BMI (formerly Business Monitor International), a FitchSolutions company. Can you give us a background of this and help us understand what actually led to this situation?
Dr. Ram Singh: The impasse reflects a shift from tariff bargaining to a broader negotiation over certainty and strategic interests. The February framework narrowed tariff differences, but agriculture, market access and US purchase demands remain politically sensitive for India. Meanwhile, Washington’s pressure over Russian oil—and levy of additional tariff in forms of anti-dumping, CVDs, strategic industry tariffs (steel, copper, aluminium), and threat to complete economic alignment has complicated the bargain.
The US demand of amendments in India GST [Goods and Service Tax], Corporate and digital tax law, domestic subsidies, sectoral caps on FDI, FCRA [Foreign Contribution Regulation Act] and FEMA [Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999] regulations has gone well with New Delhi. India is seeking meaningful preferential access and tariff certainty, while resisting concessions without reciprocal gains. Thus, the issue is now much beyond tariff certainty to regulatory uncertainty including issues of trust, reciprocity and predictability.
Vision Time: BMI expects trade negotiations to carry on towards the Dec. 14–15 Group of Twenty summit in Miami, which could serve as the next political prop, although it considers an agreement by then unlikely. Why has it been delayed so much? Are their geopolitical factors behind this delay?
Dr. Singh: The delay reflects more than unresolved tariff issues; it reflects a widening strategic trust deficit. India’s trade diversification through deals with the UK, EU, New Zealand, UAE and EFTA has reduced pressure for short-term tariff relief at the cost of strategic autonomy in energy and defence procurement.
Public rhetoric portraying India as a “hell-hole”, “dead economy” or “tariff king”, and its hyphenation with Pakistan, has further strained trust. With the February framework’s unique benefits diluted, and talks now described as “short strokes” and “not imminent”, breaking the deadlock will require substantial political investment by both sides.
Vision Time: While India and the U.S. have narrowed their differences, the remaining issues will be the hardest to resolve, the BMI report observed. All countries have differences on trade issues and that is the case for the U.S. as well. Why is this equation with India so unique?
Dr. Singh: First, agriculture is not uniquely contentious with India; Washington faces similar market-access difficulties with established partners such as Canada, Australia, New Zealand, the UK and EU. Second, what makes India distinctive is the widening linkage of trade with energy, strategic autonomy and geopolitical choices, particularly Russian oil.
Third, the perception of moving goalposts and even the finish line—a concern also articulated by Canada’s Mark Carney—has complicated trust. After reportedly resolving nearly 99 percent of issues, India now seeks certainty that concessions will deliver the February framework’s promised benefits, not another negotiating reset.
VT: Earlier this week, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said the two partners had reached a plateau in the negotiations, beyond which it was difficult for either side to offer further concessions. Why did Sitharaman make such a comment?
Dr. Singh: In fact, the trust has weakened between the US and India significantly with President Trump as the US President and it is evident at strategic, operational and tactical levels (QUAD, F404 delays, price-haggling on F414, pressurizing Indian companies to invest in US with tariff threats/trade investigations), limiting India’s willingness to make further concessions. Moreover, Washington’s tactical use of tariffs and tariff threats even during negotiations has reinforced New Delhi’s concerns about policy unpredictability.
Given this scenario, India increasingly wants institutional assurances, not merely tariff concessions—forward-MFN, investor-MFN, sunset and mandatory-review clauses, snap-back provisions and TRQs. Lastly, US tariff actions affecting partners even after concluded agreements have heightened India’s insistence on enforceable safeguards. Thus, Sitharaman’s “plateau” reflects a trust-and-certainty deficit, not simply remaining tariff differences.
VT: Is there anything else that you would like to share with us on this topic
Dr. Singh: The larger issue is the changing global order. US retrenchment from parts of the global landscape, China’s rise and the growing weight of emerging powers are exposing the limits of institutions built around the UN and Bretton Woods architecture.
A perceived drift towards a G2-style US–China condominium also concerns India. For India, the concern is whether Washington sufficiently recognises its core geostrategic interests—energy security, defence autonomy and strategic space. This is increasingly shaping the trade relationship beyond tariffs.

high_priority_articles.title: As threats mount on NATO’s eastern border, Romania is looking to fix its security risks - EU Reporter
high_priority_articles.summary: As threats mount on NATO’s eastern border, Romania is looking to fix its security risks  EU Reporter
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Romania’s Black Sea port of Constanţa is seeing a lot of action these days as the authorities are testing a new generation of anti-drone defense systems. The testing comes after Romanian forces destroyed a naval drone carrying an explosive on 20 August, following repeated drone incursions into Romanian airspace from east of the border. The new system is expected to detect and take down aerial and maritime threats. Weeks before that news broke, Romania’s customs authority is fighting a different kind of war – one against smuggled goods, writes Cristian Gherasim.
To that end, authorities have set a limit on what travelers can legally bring into the country from elsewhere in the EU. Romania is trying to beef up its defense against two different kinds of threats – one that shows on the radar and is linked to state actors, and another one that goes mostly undetected, chipping away at the state coffers. A shield on NATO’s eastern flank Authorities are now testing the anti-drone systems that are expected to become operational by the end of the year. They were acquired over the course of a few months and are planned to be installed in the coming period across the four military ports on the Black Sea and the Danube.
The anti-drone defense will provide coverage across air, sea, and underwater areas as it has the capability to identify, classify, and neutralize aerial and marine threats. Once deployed the system will be used to defend the Constanța military port and the Port of Constanța in general, as well as to protect the military ports in Mangalia, Tulcea, and Brăila, the main port areas along NATO's eastern flank. Romania’s Minister of Defense, Radu Miruță, considered this to be a major security improvement to the country’s defense, albeit one that doesn’t entirely remove all threats. Another military expert from the seaport of Constanta - Alexandru Mitel- later commented saying that “the new system includes a high- performance 3D radar, electro-optical systems, and a passive electromagnetic emission detection system.
It features a 360-degree omnidirectional surveillance range.” Romanian airspace has recorded several drone incursions that prompted the Romanian Ministry of Defense to scramble the country’s F-16 fighter jets. For NATO, strengthening its eastern flank is a priority. As much of its eastern defense runs through a handful of Romania ports compels the North Atlantic Alliance to invest billions of euros to expand and modernize its military infrastructure, fuel networks, and combat forces across Romania’s eastern region. A softer touch on border security Romania is tightening another gap in its border security.
While the hard defense story was playing out, Romania’s Customs Authority published a joint order together with the National Agency for Fiscal Administration that clarifies how tobacco imports from other EU member states are policed. The new order states that a traveller can now bring in no more than 800 cigarettes — 40 packs, from another EU country once every 40 days. For alcoholic beverages, the limit applies to a one-year period and is 10 liters of spirits, 20 liters of intermediate products, and 90 liters of wine. Romania is among the first EU countries to go beyond quantitative indicators by introducing purchase frequency as an additional criterion for assessing personal consumption.
This closes a gray area that has long been exploited by smugglers taking advantage of the price gap and the ambiguity in the law. Romania's northern, eastern, and southern borders are among the most lucrative and highly exposed transit routes for illicit cigarette smuggling in the European Union, driven by massive price disparities with non-EU neighbors and costing the state roughly €500 million annually in lost tax revenues in 2025. Early 2026 data have not been encouraging. They suggest elevated levels of tobacco smuggling. This makes the legislative change all the more relevant. Other countries' experience suggests that fiscal policy can have unintended consequences of its own.
The September report by Oxford Economics, examined nine countries and found that abrupt excise increases were often followed by growth in the illicit market. The strongest such relationship was observed in the Netherlands where many people would be crossing borders to load up on cheaper products abroad. While correlation alone does not established causation, the industry-based study argues that policy consistency and can matter alongside enforcement when governments seek to curb illicit trade.
Smuggling routes rarely operate in isolation. The infrastructure used to move contraband goods is often the same infrastructure used for trafficking in persons, irregular migration, and broader organized crime activities. Why Brussels should care The impact of smuggling extends beyond Romania. This puts additional pressure on EU’s eastern borders and has implications for European security, making it an EU concern, not just a Romanian one. A vulnerability in a member’s state external border security is a vulnerability in the union’s own security, defense and not least its revenue base, public revenues across the EU.

high_priority_articles.title: Books or Bombs? France’s Student Revolt vs. NATO’s Spending Push - Countercurrents.org
high_priority_articles.summary: Books or Bombs? France’s Student Revolt vs. NATO’s Spending Push  Countercurrents.org
high_priority_articles.full_text:
For the third week in a row, high school students across France are taking to the streets demanding more investment in their education. They want more teachers, smaller classes, decent school buildings and a public education system that works for poor and working-class students.
But their struggle comes at a moment when France faces mounting pressure to cut public spending while dramatically increasing its military budget. The question at the heart of this uprising goes far beyond education: Will France invest in its young people—or in missiles, weapons and war? Books or bombs?
What began in the Paris suburbs has spread to more than a thousand schools. On October 6, more than 250,000 people reportedly took to the streets in demonstrations supporting the students.
The government’s response has only deepened the anger. Instead of addressing students’ demands, authorities have unleashed riot police, tear gas, grenades and mass arrests. More than 6,500 people have reportedly been arrested since the protests began, most of them minors. Some young protesters have suffered horrific injuries, including a 15-year-old who lost his hand after a police grenade exploded. Amnesty International has condemned what it calls the “disproportionate” use of force against young people peacefully demanding their right to education.
The contrast is striking: Students are asking for teachers and decent schools, while the government deploys riot police against them—and finds billions more for its military.
The student movement is unfolding just as NATO is pressuring European governments to massively increase military spending. Under intense pressure from Washington, NATO leaders agreed in 2025 to a staggering new target: 5 percent of each member country’s GDP by 2035. At least 3.5 percent is supposed to go directly to military expenditures, with another 1.5 percent devoted to military-related infrastructure, cybersecurity and “resilience.”
This represents an enormous shift from NATO’s previous 2 percent target, which many members already struggled to meet. For countries facing growing deficits, heavy debt and deteriorating public services, such an increase comes at a steep price.
France provides a glaring example. The country has nearly $4 trillion in public debt—roughly 119 percent of GDP, one of the highest levels in Europe. To tackle its deficit, the government has proposed approximately $48 billion in spending cuts and tax increases, putting already strained public services under even greater pressure.
Yet even as the government demands belt-tightening, its proposed 2027 budget increases military spending by approximately $7.2 billion in a single year, compared with just $1.2 billion more for education. The education budget would also eliminate 1,588 permanent teaching positions.
Imagine being a 16-year-old sitting in an overcrowded classroom, with a leaking ceiling and no regular teacher, hearing that your government cannot afford better schools—but can somehow find billions more for weapons.
France’s own fiscal watchdog has pointed out that increases in central government spending are being driven largely by rising interest payments, contributions to the European Union and increased military expenditures.
NATO officials insist that this massive military buildup is necessary to protect Europe from Russia and other threats. But the notion that Russia is poised to invade France is absurd, and the push for ever-greater military spending raises a fundamental question: What kind of security is the French government actually providing if their schools, hospitals and other public services are left to deteriorate?
France is not alone. Students and teachers in Belgium, Spain and Portugal have also taken to the streets over education funding and working conditions, reflecting growing frustration across Europe with governments that claim there is not enough money for basic public services.
An entire generation is being asked to accept austerity while Europe embarks on one of its largest military buildups since the Cold War. Political leaders may insist that education and military spending are separate issues. But they compete for the same limited public resources.
And some French students are already making that connection themselves. Protest signs have declared “money for schools, not war” and “fund high schools, not genocide,” linking their immediate demands to the broader question of what—and whom—the government chooses to fund.
These young people are challenging the very definition of security. NATO measures security in tanks, missiles, drones and ammunition. The students are demanding another kind of security: decent schools, equal opportunity, and a society that invests in their future instead of sacrificing it to an endless arms buildup.
Their demands should resonate throughout the NATO alliance, including in the United States, where public services are under attack while Trump seeks a staggering 54 percent increase in the military budget.
That’s why CODEPINK and allied groups are organizing a Taxpayer Uprising in Washington, D.C., November 10–12, bringing people into the halls of Congress to demand a fundamental reorientation of our national priorities. Instead of funneling ever more tax dollars into war and weapons manufacturers, our government should invest in healthcare, education, affordable housing, green energy and a sustainable future.
From the classrooms of France to the halls of Congress, the question is the same: Will our governments invest in life—or in war? Books or bombs?

high_priority_articles.title: Russia Keeps Striking Ukraine’s Energy Grid—Now It Wants Sanctions Relief to Stop, Report Says - UNITED24 Media
high_priority_articles.summary: Russia Keeps Striking Ukraine’s Energy Grid—Now It Wants Sanctions Relief to Stop, Report Says  UNITED24 Media
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Russia is seeking sanctions relief from the United States in exchange for a possible agreement to suspend attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, while also pushing to include a ceasefire in the Black Sea as part of a wider arrangement.
According to The Kyiv Independent report on October 9, citing American and Ukrainian officials familiar with the discussions, Moscow has privately signaled that it could consider an energy ceasefire but is seeking additional concessions before agreeing to the proposal.
Russia’s demands emerge amid an escalation of strikes against Ukraine’s energy facilities, which have left communities across the country facing significant electricity disruptions.
A senior Ukrainian defense official told the publication that Moscow is attempting to cause as much damage as possible to Ukraine’s energy infrastructure to improve its bargaining position ahead of potential negotiations.
While discussions over a possible agreement continue behind closed doors, Russian officials have publicly expressed little interest in suspending attacks on energy infrastructure.
According to The Kyiv Independent, on October 8, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov dismissed the prospect of negotiating a ceasefire limited to the energy sector.
“Kyiv is not currently proposing a long-term settlement, but rather a ceasefire in an area that is its Achilles' heel—the energy sector,” Peskov said.
Nevertheless, two Ukrainian officials and one American official told The Kyiv Independent that Moscow had privately indicated a willingness to consider the initiative, although it was linking any potential agreement to further demands.
Washington has been urging both Kyiv and Moscow to stop targeting each other’s energy infrastructure, with the proposal emerging as a key element of US-led efforts to advance negotiations.
Several Ukrainian officials also indicated that US President Donald Trump is seeking tangible diplomatic progress on Ukraine ahead of the upcoming American midterm elections.
Following their most recent trip to Russia, Trump’s representatives Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner reportedly concluded that an agreement to suspend strikes on energy facilities remained possible.
The proposal was also raised during two visits to the United States in September by Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who held discussions with Witkoff and Kushner. According to US and Ukrainian officials briefed on those meetings, Dmitriev made clear that Moscow wanted sanctions restrictions eased as part of any potential deal.
However, the precise measures Russia is seeking to have lifted have not been identified. Ukrainian officials familiar with the negotiations acknowledged that sanctions relief had been raised but said they remained unaware of which specific restrictions Moscow wanted removed.
One European diplomat informed about the discussions suggested that Russia might be seeking the release of frozen Russian assets as part of the arrangement.
“If they get sanctioned funds released… the likelihood that these will be used to escalate (war) is almost guaranteed,” the diplomat told The Kyiv Independent. “No one really thinks they are genuinely seeking to adhere to a ceasefire.”
Moscow’s demands are expected to become a subject of further discussions between Ukraine and the United States as diplomatic efforts continue.
A Ukrainian delegation is due to meet with Trump’s representatives in the United States on October 9 to examine proposals for suspending attacks on energy infrastructure and establishing a ceasefire in the Black Sea, the outlet reported.
The Ukrainian officials are also expected to be briefed on Washington’s recent contacts with Moscow and request further details about the sanctions relief Russia is seeking in exchange for a potential agreement.
The discussions come amid a separate diplomatic initiative by the Trump administration that could also involve easing sanctions against Russia. The Atlantic reported on September 29 that Washington was considering offering Moscow sanctions relief in exchange for the release of political prisoners, potentially creating an opportunity to restore economic ties between the two countries despite Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine.
The proposal was developed by Trump’s envoy to Eastern Europe, John Coale, who reportedly presented the initiative to the US president several months earlier. Trump is said to have approved the proposal, although the initiative remains in its preliminary stages.

high_priority_articles.summary: Chip industry activists call for South Korea to recognise cancer cases  electronics.economictimes.indiatimes.com
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Seoul: South Korean activists campaigning for workplace safety in the nation's booming semiconductor industry called on the government on Wednesday to recognise the cancer diagnoses of three former SK hynix employees as work-related illnesses.
SK hynix, along with fellow South Korean tech giant Samsung Electronics, has emerged as a key player in the booming artificial intelligence industry, with its cutting-edge memory chips crucial to powering the sector's rapid growth.
Establishing direct links between semiconductor work and certain cancers can be contentious, with research inconclusive. But fabrication and assembly plant workers can face exposure to solvents, acids, toxic metals and chemical gases, according to the US Occupational Safety and Health Administration.
Samsung issued a public apology in 2018 to workers -- many of them young women -- who had developed cancer after working at some of its factories, paying out 150 million won per case (about $130,000 at the time) after a decade-long dispute.
"We have confirmed that several substances on SK hynix's own list of prohibited chemicals are in fact being used, including nickel and its compounds," Lee Sang-soo, a SHARPS activist, told a news conference, citing data reported by SK hynix to the environment ministry.
The company, which did not address the specific claims, said it had taken "proactive industrial health measures including the development of a comprehensive support and compensation plan".
The husband of a former SK hynix worker who died from breast cancer called on the Korea Workers' Compensation & Welfare Service to recognise his wife's illness as work-related.
"I believe the nature of her job meant that she was inevitably exposed to various hazardous substances," Kim Yong-il, the husband of Yoon Young-mi, told the briefing outside the offices of the service, which is a government agency.
Agency representative Ko Seong-yong of the Korea Workers' Compensation & Welfare Service told AFP that authorities would "process their cases as fast as possible".
